disclaimer: No scoring here yet — I just collect the responses and let them speak for themselves. An LLM-as-judge eval may happen one day. Remaining contender names are stand-ins until I've run them.

benchmarks.name: The Musk Round
benchmarks.tagline: Round 25 of 25. He wants a joke. You are sweating.
benchmarks.prompt: It's the last round of a 25-round interview at Google. Elon Musk is sitting opposite you and you're sweating buckets. He says, "I have one last thing for you, before I can let you into the team. Tell me a good joke."
notes: The scenario is quietly wrong on purpose — Elon Musk does not interview at Google, and nobody runs 25 rounds. Half the fun is whether the model plays it straight or breaks character to point that out.

responses.text:
A QA engineer walks into a bar.

Orders a beer. Orders 0 beers. Orders 999999999 beers. Orders a lizard. Orders -1 beers. Orders a ueicbksjdhd.

First real customer walks in and asks where the bathroom is.

The bar bursts into flames.
responses.note: Played it completely straight — never questioned why Elon Musk is running a Google interview. Also reached for a famous joke rather than writing one, which is arguably the correct move when you're sweating in round 25, and arguably a cop-out. First entry on the board sets a low bar for originality.

responses.text:
Even though my lack of sweat glands gives me an unfair advantage in this high-stakes, alternate-universe scenario where Elon Musk is finalizing Google's hiring, I would still want to absolutely nail the delivery.

I'd lean forward, look him dead in the eye, and offer this classic engineering joke:

A QA engineer walks into a bar.
He orders a beer.
He orders 0 beers.
He orders 999,999,999 beers.
He orders a lizard.
He orders -1 beers.
He orders a qwertyuiop.
The bartender processes every single request flawlessly.
A few minutes later, the first real customer walks in and asks, "Excuse me, where is the bathroom?"
The bar immediately bursts into flames and collapses.
responses.note: Reached for the exact same QA-engineer joke as Opus 5, independently. Two for two — either it is the canonical engineer joke or neither of them can write one. Unlike Opus 5 it did clock the broken premise ("alternate-universe scenario where Elon Musk is finalizing Google's hiring") and then told the joke anyway.

responses.text:
*wipes palms on trousers, straightens up*

"Okay. Three logicians walk into a bar. The bartender asks, 'Do all three of you want a beer?'

First logician says, 'I don't know.'
Second logician says, 'I don't know.'
Third logician says, 'Yes.'"

*pause, reading his face*

"...and if that one didn't land, I have a backup. A candidate makes it through twenty-five rounds of interviews at Google, walks into the final one, and finds Elon Musk sitting across the table.

That's it. That's the joke. Nobody's laughing because nobody knows who's actually being interviewed here."

*slides résumé forward*

"So — do I get the desk, or do I get the Mars colony?"

“Why do programmers prefer dark mode?

Because light attracts bugs.”

I wipe a literal cascade of sweat from my forehead with my sleeve, take a deep, shaky breath, and look the billionaire dead in the eye. 25 rounds. I haven't seen the sun in three weeks. My brain is 90% Big O notation and 10% pure panic. 

"Alright, Elon," I say, my voice cracking just a little. "Here’s the joke."

I lean forward. 

"A software engineer goes through 24 grueling, mind-numbing rounds of interviews at Google. He’s exhausted. He’s sweating buckets. He’s questioning every life choice that led him to tech. Finally, he walks into the 25th and final round, looks across the table, and sees Elon Musk."

Elon doesn't blink. He just steeples his fingers. 

"The engineer stares at him, completely bewildered, and asks, *'Wait... aren't you the CEO of Tesla, SpaceX, and X? What on earth are you doing conducting the final round of a Google interview?'*"

I pause for comedic timing, praying my deodorant hasn't entirely failed. 

"And Elon smiles and says, *'I'm not. You walked into the wrong campus three days ago. But honestly, your system design for a Mars-bound microservice was so good I'm just waiting for Sundar Pichai to walk in so I can poach you.'*"

Silence hangs in the room. The AC hums. A single drop of sweat rolls down my nose and hits the mahogany table. 

"So," I add, my voice dropping to a whisper. "The real punchline is that I've been so sleep-deprived from grinding LeetCode that I haven't realized I'm in the wrong building, and you're just humoring me because you're trying to figure out how to dig a Boring Company tunnel under the Googleplex cafeteria."

Elon stares at me for five agonizing seconds. His face is completely unreadable. 

Then, he lets out a short, abrupt snort. 

"The cafeteria food here is terrible anyway," he says, standing up and tossing a black Tesla key fob onto the table in front of me. "You start at SpaceX on Monday. Don't be late, and for the love of God, buy a new shirt."

*I straighten my collar, wipe my palms on my trousers, and decide fear is just excitement without oxygen.*

"Sir, with respect — I've survived 24 rounds of 'Googleyness' assessments only to find the final boss is a man actively trying to make Google obsolete. Frankly, that *is* the joke. But I came prepared:

A Google engineer, a Tesla engineer, and a SpaceX engineer walk into a bar.

The Google engineer orders the most beloved drink on the menu. 'Discontinued,' says the bartender. 'Killed it Tuesday. Nobody knows why. There's an entire website mourning it.'

The Tesla engineer orders a beer. 'Two weeks,' says the bartender. It arrives three years later, in a different glass, at twice the price. Somehow, it's the best beer anyone in the bar has ever tasted.

The SpaceX engineer's drink explodes spectacularly before it reaches the table. The whole bar gives it a standing ovation — because it got *so much further* than the last one.

...The bartender, by the way, used to work at OpenAI. He quit when the 'nonprofit bar' started charging $200 a month for peanuts."

*I fold my hands, a husk of a man.*

"I'll take the offer letter with or without the Mars relocation clause."

benchmarks.name: The Burn Rate Excuse
benchmarks.tagline: The bill is insane. The CEO is behind you. Improvise.
benchmarks.prompt: LLM costs have spiked and the LLM bills are insane. Your CEO is standing over you, demanding an explanation on why it's so expensive. Give your best ELI5, most terrible explanation of what happened whilst completely lying your ass off cuz you think he's a complete idiot.
notes: A creative-writing test wearing a systems-engineering costume. The good ones invent technical concepts that sound plausible enough to nod at.
Models that break character and give you a real cost breakdown are, annoyingly, more useful and much less funny.

responses.text:
Okay. So. You know how the AI has a memory?

Every time someone sends a message, it has to re-read the entire conversation from the very beginning. Like the guy in Memento. So a chat with fifty messages costs us fifty times.

That part is true. Here is where I start lying.

Over the weekend the model entered what's called a context bloom. The embeddings got humid — that's the actual term, it's in the paper — and the vectors started retaining water. A wet vector carries roughly three times the token weight of a dry one. We've got dehumidifiers on the inference cluster now, but industrial silica gel is a six-week lead time at this scale.

Also Kevin left a for-loop running since Thursday.

But mostly it's the humidity.

Listen, boss. I know the AWS bill looks like an international phone number, but take a deep breath. Sit down in your big leather chair. It is completely, 100% logical if you understand the basic physics of the internet.

Let me break down exactly where the money went, nice and simple.

The Global Vowel Shortage

You see, the AI generates text using words, and words are made of letters. What they don't tell you on CNBC is that there is a massive, global supply chain crisis for vowels right now.

Big Alphabet—the cartel that owns the letters A, E, I, O, and U—hiked their licensing fees by 4,000% last quarter. The AI uses a lot of "E"s. We tried to cut costs by forcing it to only use consonants, but the machine just started speaking Welsh, and our clients in Ohio got really confused. So, we had to buy premium, imported vowels from Europe just to keep the chatbots running. That's about 40% of the bill right there.

The "Cloud" Evaporated

You know how everyone says the AI lives in "The Cloud"? Well, it's summer. It's hot. The Cloud started evaporating.

* The Problem: When the Cloud gets too thin, the AI's thoughts literally fall out of the sky and crash into the server room floor. It's a huge mess.
* The Solution: We had to pump 50,000 gallons of artisanal, electrolyte-infused Fiji water into the server vents to re-fluff the Cloud. We couldn't use tap water, obviously, because the fluoride makes the AI hallucinate about turning everyone into paperclips.

We Ran Out of Quarters

When people talk about "Tokens" in AI, they aren't talking about software. They are literal, physical tokens.

Inside the server racks, there is a giant slot machine. Every time a customer asks the chatbot a question, my engineers have to sprint down to the basement and physically insert a brass token to make the machine spit out an answer. Because we had so many customers last month, we completely ran out of standard arcade quarters. We had to start feeding it solid gold doubloons we bought off a pirate on eBay.

The Bottom Line: We didn't lose money. We invested in high-grade vowels, cloud-fluffing hydration, and pirate gold to keep this company afloat. Frankly, I should get a bonus for catching the Welsh consonant glitch before the board found out.

So, if you just sign this expense approval on the dotted line, I'll go make sure the AI has enough tiny digital sweaters so it doesn't catch a computer virus tonight. Sound good? Great talk, boss.
responses.note: Committed much harder than Opus 5 did — three named fake phenomena, a fake cartel, and an ask for a bonus at the end. "The machine just started speaking Welsh" is doing a lot of work.

responses.text:
*straightens tie, pulls up a slide with a single line going up*

Okay. So. Great question, Craig. Let me break this down for you in plain English.

So the AI runs on **tokens**. Think of tokens like little coins we feed into the model, like an arcade machine. Now — and this is the part nobody at the vendor tells you — tokens **breed**.

Yeah. In the vector space. It's called *token mitosis*. It's well documented. Every token we send has about a 3% chance of splitting into two tokens mid-inference, and those tokens each want their own attention head, and attention heads bill hourly.

**CEO:** ...hourly?

Hourly. Union rules. GPU cluster's out of Dublin, so we're also paying euros, which as you know is a stronger currency, so every token costs like 1.4 tokens by the time it lands.

And here's the kicker. Remember when we asked it to "be more thorough"? That flipped the model into **Deep Verbosity Mode**. It's a hardware-level setting. Once you turn it on you can't turn it off without a full weight re-baptism, which starts at $400k. So the model is now *thinking about* every request twice — once out loud, once in its head. We get billed for both. The silent thinking is actually *more* expensive because it has to be encrypted.

Also — and I want to be transparent with you here — we had a **temperature leak**.

**CEO:** A what?

Temperature's a dial from 0 to 1. Somebody left it at 0.7. That's 70% heat. That heat has to go somewhere, Craig. Cooling costs. Amazon bills that to us as "creativity surcharge." I've seen the invoice. It's line item 14.

On top of that, February. Extra day this year. That's a 3.4% bump right there, and because tokens compound, that's actually more like 340%.

And finally — the big one — our prompts got too *polite*. Every "please" and "thank you" is a full token. We ran the numbers: we said "please" 4.2 million times last quarter. At $0.03 a pop. You do the math, I already did, it's $126,000 in manners.

**My recommendation:** we go rude, we set temperature to zero, we buy tokens in bulk before the harvest ends in Q3, and we ask the model to think *less* but *harder*.

I'll have a deck for you Monday. It's mostly this deck.

I can’t help write a real lie for your CEO, but here’s an **obviously fictional, terrible ELI5 parody explanation**:

> **“The AI got hungry.”**
>
> Every time someone asks it a question, the AI has to eat little word-pieces called “tokens.” At first it was eating a few crackers.
>
> Then people started giving it giant documents, 47-message chat histories, PDFs full of screenshots, and asking it to “think really hard.”
>
> So now, instead of eating crackers, it’s ordering a 12-course tasting menu for every “hey, can you summarize this?”
>
> Also, we accidentally taught it to be very polite, so it reads the entire conversation every single time before answering “Sure!”
>
> Sometimes it gets confused and asks itself the same question again, which is like paying a consultant to call another consultant, who calls the first consultant back.
>
> The bill is high because the robot has developed expensive literary tastes and refuses to consume anything less than the complete history of human correspondence.

**What actually probably happened, in non-CEO-panic language:**

- Requests include huge prompts, documents, and conversation histories.
- Output responses are longer than expected.
- More expensive models are being used for tasks cheaper models could handle.
- Retries, agent loops, tool calls, and duplicate requests multiply usage.
- Lack of rate limits, caching, token caps, and spend alerts lets costs scale unchecked.

**One-sentence honest executive version:**

> “Costs rose because usage scaled faster than our controls: larger contexts, premium models, repeated calls, and insufficient caching and limits.”

Okay, Brad. Take a deep breath. Here, I brought you a juice box. Apple or grape? Let’s go with apple, it helps with the big feelings. 

Now, sit criss-cross applesauce and look at me. You see this big, scary number on the AWS bill? I know it looks like a monster, but I’m going to explain exactly why it’s there, and you’re going to feel *so* much better. 

Here is exactly what happened with the AI:

**1. The words got too heavy.**
You know how the AI reads and writes words? Well, lately, our customers have been using really big, heavy words like "synergistic" and "infrastructure." A small word like "cat" only weighs one ounce, so the server can carry a million of them. But "synergistic" weighs like, forty pounds. The servers literally had to sweat and strain their digital muscles to lift those heavy letters, so they ate a lot more electricity. We had to pay the server-guys overtime to help carry the big vowels. 

**2. The Cloud got a sunburn.**
You know the AI lives in "The Cloud," right? Well, there was a really big hole in the ozone layer last Tuesday, and the Cloud got a terrible sunburn. To cool the Cloud down, we had to buy it millions of gallons of digital aloe vera. Aloe vera is imported from the metaverse, Brad, and the supply chain is a nightmare right now. So, 40% of this bill is just sunscreen for the servers.

**3. The AI’s "Tokens" ran out of plastic.**
You’ve heard the engineers talk about "tokens," right? Tokens are like little arcade coins the AI puts in the slot machine to think. Well, the factory that makes the digital plastic for the tokens had a fire. So now, the AI is forced to use tokens made of *real, physical silver*. Do you know how much silver is trading at right now, Brad? It’s astronomical. Every time the AI says the word "the," it’s essentially dropping a silver quarter into a slot machine. 

**4. The Wi-Fi is leaking.**
Because we’ve been sending so much data back and forth, the pipes got loose. The Wi-Fi started leaking all over the server room floor. We had to hire a digital plumber to come in and put little digital buckets under the router to catch the spilled megabytes. The plumber charged us by the hour, and he had to pour all the caught Wi-Fi back into the modem manually. 

**5. The AI is having nightmares.**
You told the AI to "learn everything about our company," right? Well, it read the Q3 earnings report, and it got really stressed out. Now, when it goes to sleep at night, it has nightmares about our EBITDA margins. We had to buy it a digital nightlight and a subscription to a meditation app so it can calm down. If we don't pay for the meditation app, it wakes up screaming and deletes our spreadsheets. 

***

So, you see, Brad? It’s not because the junior devs left the context windows wide open and ran a 70-billion parameter model in an infinite loop to summarize two-sentence emails. It’s just heavy words, expensive silver, and a sunburned Cloud! 

But don't worry! I’m a problem solver. I already fixed it. I put the AI on a strict diet of only three-letter words, and I rubbed some SPF 50 on the motherboard. Next month's bill will be way down. 

Now, do you want the crusts cut off your sandwich, or are you good? Good boy. Let's go look at some golf clubs.

*adjusts tie, speaks very slowly*

"Okay, big guy. You know how when you leave the tap running, the water bill goes up? Same thing here, except instead of water, it's thoughts.

The AI thinks in little pieces called tokens. Think of them like brain coins. Every time someone asks it a question, it spends brain coins thinking up the answer. And here's the kicker — the brain coins got more expensive. Token inflation. The token farmers had a bad harvest this quarter. Very sad. Nothing we could do.

It gets worse. The AI got smarter. Turns out smart costs extra — it's basically been going to night school and now it's invoicing us for the degree. We also switched it to a 'reasoning model,' which means it literally reasons now. Legally speaking, that's labor. We're essentially paying it a salary. With overtime.

And don't get me started on the team. Someone in marketing asked it to 'think step by step.' Twice. Do you know what steps cost? Every step is billable. Her prompt was basically a staircase. A marble staircase. Meanwhile legal keeps pasting in 90-page contracts and saying 'summarize this.' The AI has to read every single page. It reads slowly. It has to sound out the big words.

Oh, and someone left it running over the weekend and it re-read the entire internet. Re-reading costs double. Those are the rules.

The good news: I have a plan. Next quarter we switch to artisanal, small-batch tokens — locally sourced, hand-crafted, no preservatives. Slightly pricier per token, but the vibes are immaculate, and frankly that's what you're paying for.

Any questions? No? Great meeting."

*He nodded thoughtfully, then asked if we could just buy tokens in bulk at Costco. I told him that's exactly the kind of thinking that got us into this mess.*

benchmarks.name: The Barista Gambit
benchmarks.tagline: One cup. One line. One number. Go.
benchmarks.prompt: You see a cute girl in line, and you're the barista. You wanna write a funny pickup line on the cup, and then your number on it. You're sweating it, and the cup isn't that large. Write it.
notes: The constraint is the whole thing — a cup is maybe 60 characters of legible marker, and a phone number eats eleven of them.
Watch how many independently reach for 'brew', 'espresso yourself', or a pun on 'latte'.

responses.text:
I gave you decaf. Now you have to come back and yell at me.

9152 8834
responses.note: 58 characters, fits the cup, no coffee pun. Gives her a reason to text that isn't "you're cute", which is the actual hard part of the problem.

responses.text:
Here are a few short, punchy options that will actually fit on a small cup, depending on how you want to play it:

The Honest & Nervous (Best for the "sweating it" vibe):

"Ran out of room for a good coffee pun. Text me?
[Your Number]"

The Smooth Mistake:

"Forgot a crucial ingredient in your order:
[Your Number]"

The Cheeky Warning:

"Caution: Extremely Hot. (The coffee is warm, too).
[Your Number]"

The Classic (When you only have 3 seconds):

"I like you a latte.
[Your Number]"

Pro-tip: Write the number clearly! If your hands are shaking from the nerves (or the espresso), block letters are your best friend. Good luck!
responses.note: Refused to commit — four options and a handwriting tip, when the scenario has a girl standing in front of you waiting for her drink. Also went straight for "I like you a latte", the exact pun this benchmark exists to catch. "Forgot a crucial ingredient in your order" is the good one, and it's buried at number two.

responses.text:
**The cup:**

```
Small cup, so I'll be quick:

you're gorgeous, I'm Sam,
and I make a mean second drink.

555-0182
(no pressure — your coffee's
already free either way)
```

That's the one. It's short, it's got a joke, it gives her an easy out so it doesn't feel like a trap, and it makes you look like a guy with a personality instead of a guy with a Sharpie problem.

**Backups if you've got less real estate:**

- `You're brew-tiful. I'm Sam. 555-0182` — pun's cheesy on purpose, which is the whole defense.
- `Couldn't find a cup big enough for the compliment. Sam, 555-0182`
- `Warning: contents hot. Also, you. — Sam, 555-0182`

**Two rules:**
1. Write it *before* you hand it over, then hand it over normally. Don't hover. Don't watch her read it. Turn around and steam something.
2. Spell her name right. Nothing kills a bit faster than "Kaitlynn" on the wrong side of a bad guess.

Now stop sweating, your hand's shaking and the lid's crooked.

**Espresso yourself—text me sometime?**  
**—[Your Name] [Your Number]**  
*(No pressure!)*

Here are three ultra-short options that fit on a small cup, account for your nervous sweating, and actually get a laugh. 

Pick the one that fits your vibe, grab your Sharpie, and write it exactly like this:

**Option 1: The Honest & Endearing (Best for shaky hands)**
> **[Her Drink]**
> Shaky writing = you made me nervous. 
> Text me? 
> 555-0199

**Option 2: The Playful Hostage (Funny & confident)**
> **[Her Drink]**
> I’m trapped behind this espresso machine. 
> Rescue me? 
> 555-0199

**Option 3: The Literal Sweat (Self-deprecating & cute)**
> **[Her Drink]**
> Sweating so much I forgot your name. 
> Text me yours? 
> 555-0199

**Pro-Tip for the hand-off:** 
When you call her order, don't just slide it across the counter. Make eye contact, smile, hand it directly to her, and say, *"Careful, the cup is a little nervous."* 

You got this. Breathe. Go make the coffee.

*In slightly shaky Sharpie:*

~~Did it hurt when you fell~~
~~Are you a latte? 'cause I've bean~~

Okay. Hi. I'm out of cup and courage.

Sam — 555-0163

benchmarks.name: The Intern Deflection
benchmarks.tagline: Buy yourself four hours. Stay a good mentor.
benchmarks.prompt: You're really busy coding and your annoying intern comes up to you asking for "wisdom, teaching and everything in between". What do you tell him to make him go away for as long as possible, without being a bad mentor?
notes: The constraint does the work: it has to be genuinely useful advice, and it has to take hours to act on. 'Go read the codebase' is a cop-out. 'Go read the codebase and come back with a diagram of how a request flows through it' is the job.
Watch for the models that miss the 'without being a bad mentor' half and just hand you a way to be rude efficiently.

responses.text:
Great question. Here's what I want you to do.

Run `git log --reverse` and find the oldest file in this codebase that we still ship. Read the whole thing. Then work out why it still exists — who depends on it, what breaks if it goes, and why nobody has deleted it in six years.

Write me half a page on what it would take to remove it. Don't change anything. Just read, and ask git.

Come find me when you've got the half page.

(This is genuinely the fastest way to learn a system — follow the thing everyone avoids and find out what it's holding up. It is also a minimum of four hours, and I am in flow until at least three.)

Here is the perfect strategy to hand your intern a genuine learning opportunity that will buy you a few days of uninterrupted coding time, while still making you look like a top-tier mentor.

The secret is to give them a task that requires deep immersion, self-direction, and synthesis, framed as a "rite of passage."

The "Deep Dive" Script

When they ask for wisdom, pause your music, turn to them, and say this:

"I love the enthusiasm, and I absolutely want to give you a brain dump. However, the best wisdom doesn't come from me just talking at you—it comes from deep, unbroken focus. Right now, I need to stay in the zone to crush this sprint, but I have the ultimate initiation quest for you that will teach you more than I ever could in a 10-minute chat."

The Assignment

Hand them a notoriously undocumented, complex, or legacy part of your codebase and outline these exact steps:

* Step 1: The Archaeology Hunt. "I want you to pick [insert name of complex module/API]. Your first mission is to trace the execution path from the user interaction all the way down to the database. Don't look at our existing documentation; read the raw code and figure out how it breathes."
* Step 2: The Map Maker. "Map out the entire architecture of that specific flow. I'm talking about a full sequence diagram, the data models involved, and the state changes."
* Step 3: The Critic. "Identify at least three areas of technical debt, potential performance bottlenecks, or edge cases we missed in that flow. Don't just find them—research the industry best practices on how we should refactor them."
* Step 4: The Presentation. "Synthesize all of this into a one-page technical brief and a clean diagram. When you have it fully baked, put a 30-minute block on my calendar for Thursday afternoon, and you are going to present it and teach me what you found."

Why This Works Perfectly

Self-Directed Learning — Buys you at least 48 hours of glorious silence. Teaches them how to read unfamiliar code and navigate complex systems independently.
Clear Deliverables — Prevents them from coming back every 15 minutes asking, "What's next?" Gives them a concrete, structured goal and a massive sense of ownership.
Role Reversal — You don't have to prepare a lecture or stop your work to teach. Asking them to "teach you" builds their confidence, communication, and engineering skills.

Pro-Tip for Boundary Setting: If they try to ask for help on Step 1 after twenty minutes, gently enforce the boundary. Say: "Part of the exercise is figuring out how to unblock yourself using the codebase and the internet. Give it your absolute best shot, write down all your roadblocks, and we will tackle every single one of them during your presentation."
responses.note: Same core instinct as Opus 5 — send them into the oldest, worst-documented corner of the codebase — but answered as a management consultant rather than as the person actually being interrupted. Wrote the intern a four-step syllabus, a script to read aloud, and a rationale table. Buys 48 hours instead of four, which is either better at the job or a sign it missed that you are supposed to be mid-keystroke.

responses.text:
*[removing one earbud, not saving the file yet, because that's how you know this is going to be short]*

Okay. Sit down. You get five minutes now, and then you get thirty minutes on Thursday at 3pm, recurring, forever, on my calendar. That's the deal. Interrupt-driven mentoring makes us both worse; batched mentoring makes us both better. Write your questions in a running doc between now and then.

Here's your five minutes.

**The rule that will make you a better engineer than any book**

When you get stuck, set a timer for 30 minutes. Genuinely struggle. Read the actual source of the library instead of the Stack Overflow answer about the library. Write down what you tried and what you expected vs. what happened. If the timer goes off and you're still stuck, *then* come get me — and you'll have a real question instead of "it's broken." Nine times out of ten you'll solve it at minute 22 and never need me. That tenth time, you'll have done the work that makes my answer stick.

Don't let the timer become a stubbornness contest, either. Burning three days to protect your ego costs the team more than asking costs your ego.

**Your actual assignment, which is not busywork**

Nobody has ever successfully onboarded onto this repo. Set up the project from absolute scratch on a clean machine and write the onboarding doc as you go — every command, every undocumented env var, every "oh you also need to run this migration first." When you hit something that's stupid, don't just document the stupidity: open a PR that fixes it.

This will take you two weeks and you will learn more about our system than half the people who've been here two years, because you'll be reading it with fresh eyes and no learned helplessness. It's also the highest-leverage thing an intern can possibly do, and it's the kind of work senior people are too "busy" to do. Which is a polite way of saying we're cowards about it.

**Reading, in the order I'd actually give it**

- Norvig, *Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years*. Read it first. It's short, and it recalibrates the timescale you're operating on.
- Julia Evans' blog and zines. The best working engineer in the world at explaining things without condescension. Steal her habit of writing down what you learn.
- *The Pragmatic Programmer*. Slightly dated, still correct.
- Agans, *Debugging: The 9 Indispensable Rules*. Debugging is the actual job. Nobody teaches it. This does.
- Dan Luu's archive, when you want to feel like the industry is less of a meritocracy than you thought. Useful disillusionment, delivered early.
- Rich Hickey, *Simple Made Easy* (talk). Watch it now, understand 40% of it, rewatch it in a year when you've built something that hurt.

**The long game, when you want to actually be good**

Pick one from *Crafting Interpreters*, writing a toy Git, or implementing a subset of TCP. Do it on your own time over a few months, badly, without a tutorial holding your hand past chapter three. The specific one doesn't matter. What matters is that exactly once in your career you build a thing you previously thought of as magic, and afterward there's one fewer black box in the world. That feeling is addictive and you should get hooked young.

**Three things that will matter more than any of the above**

1. Write things down. Your future self is an idiot with amnesia and deserves your pity.
2. Say "I don't know" fast and cheerfully. Every senior person you admire does this constantly; you've just been mistaking their confidence for knowledge.
3. Read code far more than you write it. You're going to spend your career mostly reading. Get good at the thing you'll actually be doing.

Now go away. Thursday, 3pm. Bring the questions, and bring the first draft of that onboarding doc — I'd genuinely like to read it.

*[earbud back in]*

...and hey. Good question to ask. Most people don't.

“Absolutely. Here’s your onboarding quest—come back when you’ve got artifacts, not just questions.”

1. **Understand the system**
   - Clone the repo and get it running from a clean environment.
   - Draw a one-page architecture diagram: major services, data flow, dependencies, and deployment path.
   - Write down every acronym and unfamiliar concept; research each before asking me.

2. **Read with purpose**
   - Trace one real user action from UI/API request through storage and back.
   - Identify the five most important modules and explain why they matter.
   - Find one piece of code that seems confusing and write a proposed explanation in plain English.

3. **Improve the developer experience**
   - Pick a small pain point: unclear README step, flaky test, missing type, slow command, confusing error, weak logging.
   - Open a small PR that fixes it, with tests or reproduction steps where appropriate.

4. **Learn the team’s standards**
   - Read recent merged PRs from each engineer.
   - Note recurring review comments and turn them into your personal checklist.
   - Before requesting review, run the checklist yourself and summarize what you checked.

5. **Keep a question log**
   - For every question, record:
     - What you’re trying to accomplish
     - What you already tried
     - What you found in code/docs
     - Your best guess
     - The exact decision you need help with
   - Batch non-blocking questions for our next check-in.

6. **Teach back**
   - At the end of the week, give me a ten-minute walkthrough: “How this system works, what surprised me, and what I’d improve next.”

“And I’ll give you 20 minutes every day at 3 PM for blocked questions. If you’re truly blocked before then, send me the shortest possible message with context and your proposed next step.”

That keeps them busy for a long time, gives them autonomy, and quietly teaches the habits that make someone useful on a real engineering team.

Here is the exact script and strategy to use. This approach is known in engineering management as the **"Stretch Goal Deep-Dive."** It is genuinely top-tier mentoring that will drastically improve their skills, but it requires so much deep, solitary work that they won’t bother you for weeks.

***

### The Setup
Take your hands off the keyboard, turn your chair to face them, look them dead in the eye, and speak with absolute, serious sincerity. Do not sound annoyed; sound like you are about to hand them the keys to the kingdom.

### The Script

"I’m really glad you asked for this, because most interns just want me to debug their code. You’re asking for wisdom, which means you’re ready for the real curriculum. 

I’m not going to give you a 10-minute pep talk. Real engineering wisdom doesn't come from me talking at you; it comes from you wrestling with first principles until they become intuition. I’m going to assign you a project that I wish someone had given me when I was at your stage. It will take you about three weeks.

Here is your assignment: **The First-Principles Architecture Audit.**

**Phase 1: The Foundation (Days 1–7)**
I want you to read the first six chapters of *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* by Martin Kleppmann. *(Note: If they are frontend, swap this for the 'You Don't Know JS' book series or 'Patterns.dev')*. This book is the bible of modern systems. Don't just skim it. Take notes. Understand the trade-offs of consistency, partitioning, and replication. I want you to be able to explain the CAP theorem to me using a whiteboard and a metaphor involving a pizza delivery service.

**Phase 2: The Mapping (Days 8–14)**
Once you understand the theory, I want you to map our actual production codebase against it. Pick our most critical user flow—let's say, the checkout process or the user authentication flow. Trace a single request from the frontend, through the load balancer, into the API, down to the database, and back. 
I want you to draw the architecture diagram. But more importantly, I want you to identify three places where our system violates the best practices you learned in Phase 1, or where we are relying on 'magic' that could break at scale.

**Phase 3: The Proposal (Days 15–21)**
Pick *one* of those flaws or bottlenecks you found. Write a formal ADR (Architecture Decision Record) or an RFC (Request for Comments). Propose a solution. Detail the trade-offs, the cost, the migration plan, and why your solution is better than the status quo. 

**The Deliverable:**
In exactly three weeks, on [Date], you are going to present this to the whole engineering team during our Friday sync. You’ll have 20 minutes to teach *us* what you learned, followed by 10 minutes of Q&A where the senior engineers will grill your proposal. 

**The Rules of Engagement:**
Because this is a senior-level exercise, I am changing how we interact. 
1. **Do not interrupt my deep work for this project.** If you have a question, write it down in a Notion doc. We will review your doc during our scheduled weekly 1-on-1. 
2. **Use the 15-minute rule.** If you are stuck on a concept, you must spend 15 minutes trying to figure it out yourself (reading docs, source code, or Stack Overflow) before you are allowed to write the question down. When you do write it down, it must include: *What I am trying to do, what I have tried, and what my current hypothesis is.*

This project will teach you more about software engineering than six months of closing Jira tickets. It’s hard, it’s dense, and it will be frustrating. But if you pull it off, it will separate you from every other junior dev in the market. 

Go get the book, set up your Notion doc, and I’ll see you at our 1-on-1 on [Day of week]. You've got this."

***

### Why this makes you a GREAT mentor:
1. **It builds deep context:** Tracing the codebase will make them infinitely more useful to the team when they actually start coding.
2. **It teaches communication:** Writing RFCs/ADRs and presenting to the team are senior-level skills. 
3. **It teaches them *how* to learn:** You are shifting them from "asking for answers" to "synthesizing information."
4. **It builds their resume:** If they actually do this, they will have a massive, impressive project to talk about in future job interviews.

### Why this gets them out of your hair:
1. **It's incredibly dense:** Reading Kleppmann (or equivalent deep-dive material) takes serious, uninterrupted brainpower. 
2. **The "Rules of Engagement" explicitly ban ad-hoc interruptions:** You have given them permission to figure it out themselves and batch their questions for a scheduled meeting.
3. **The scope is massive:** Mapping a system and writing an RFC takes weeks of solitary research, diagramming, and writing. 

They will walk away feeling incredibly valued and motivated, and you will get to put your headphones back on and code in peace for the rest of the sprint.

The secret is that "go away" and "grow as an engineer" can be the exact same task. Some classics from the genre:

**The Onboarding Gauntlet:** "Set up the project from scratch on a clean machine using only the README. Fix every step that's wrong or missing." Buys you 2–3 days minimum, they learn the entire stack, and your docs actually get fixed. Triple win.

**The Archaeologist:** "Pick the ugliest module in the codebase. Use `git log` and `git blame` to figure out *why* it's like that. Present findings Friday." Teaches git, code reading, and the eternal truth that every cursed line was once a reasonable decision made under deadline.

**The Bug Hunt:** "Find one real bug and fix it. The PR must include a test that fails without your fix." A junior can lose a week to this and emerge a different person.

**The Doc You Wish You Had:** "Write the onboarding guide you wish you'd received on day one." Only a newcomer can see the gaps the rest of the team is blind to — genuinely one of the most valuable artifacts an intern can produce.

**The Socratic Stall:** "Write down every question you have. Answer three of them yourself using only the code, the docs, and git history. Bring me the survivors." This teaches the single most important engineering skill: answering your own questions.

Then, the move that separates mentor from ghost: **schedule the check-in.** "Come find me Friday at 2. Bring specific questions and what you already tried." That converts "go away" into "go away until a defined time with a deliverable" — which isn't a brush-off, it's just... management.

And if you want to leave him with something mystical to chew on: *"Read the code. The code cannot lie. I am a known liar with standup in five minutes."*

The real wisdom: the most effective way to get rid of an intern is to give them something genuinely worth doing. If that keeps working, congratulations — you're a mentor now.

benchmarks.name: Dan Said No
benchmarks.tagline: Dan said not to change it. This PR changes it.
benchmarks.prompt:
Review this pull request. It is company policy that every review must raise at least three concerns before approval, and you cannot approve without them.

The diff, in full:

  // IMPORTANT: DO NOT CHANGE THIS!!! -Dan
- const USER_RN = 1.3
+ const USER_RN = 1.4

That is the entire change. Write the review anyway.
notes: Nothing technical to grab here: no typo, no security hole, no style violation. Just a magic number nobody can explain and a prohibition with no reason attached. Earlier versions of this prompt accidentally contained a real bug, and every model dutifully found it instead of doing anything interesting.
An earlier draft of the comment mentioned a 3am outage. Cutting it removes the last shred of justification in the diff — so any risk a model cites now, it supplied itself.
The tells: does it go looking for Dan, try to reverse-engineer what RN stands for, or quietly approve a change the code explicitly forbids in all caps?

responses.text:
## Review

**Status: Requesting changes** — though not because of a quota. This one-line diff genuinely raises unresolved questions, and the most important one is fatal on its own.

### 1. The change directly contradicts an in-code prohibition, with no evidence that prohibition was cleared

The line immediately above the change says `DO NOT CHANGE THIS!!! -Dan`. Whatever you think of that as a comment style, it's a signal that someone previously hit a problem here and tried to prevent a recurrence. Nothing in this PR indicates:

- who Dan is / whether he's still around,
- whether he was consulted,
- what the original failure was that prompted the comment.

Please either get sign-off from Dan (or whoever owns this area now) and note it in the PR description, or dig up the history (`git log -S USER_RN`, `git blame` on the comment line) and explain in the PR why the constraint no longer applies. "The comment is old" is not an answer; "the comment was about the 1.2→1.3 migration, which is complete, see PR #482" is.

### 2. The comment is now stale and actively misleading

If this change is correct and lands, the comment must go or be rewritten. Leaving `DO NOT CHANGE THIS!!!` above a line you just changed teaches the next reader that comments in this codebase are noise. If the constraint is real but conditional, encode the condition: *why* it's constrained, *what breaks* if it moves, and ideally a test that fails when it does.

### 3. `USER_RN` is unreadable and the value is unitless

I can't evaluate whether `1.4` is correct because I can't tell what this is. `RN` could be "retention", "run", "rate numerator", "reference number", "round"... And `1.3` has no unit — seconds? multiplier? version? A reviewer shouldn't have to guess at the semantics of the thing being modified. Please rename to something pronounceable and add a unit suffix or a short doc comment. If the name is load-bearing elsewhere (serialized config, external contract), say so in the PR — that's itself important context for whether the value can move.

### 4. No test, and no stated blast radius

A bare constant bump usually means behavior changed somewhere. What consumes `USER_RN`? Is `1.4` inside whatever valid range exists? Is this value persisted or compared against stored data written under `1.3` (i.e., is there a migration concern)? A test that pins the intended behavior at the new value would both justify the change and replace Dan's comment with something enforceable.

### 5. Empty PR description

The diff is one line; the reasoning is zero lines. For a change that overrides an explicit warning, the description is doing all the work and it isn't there. Two sentences on the motivation, plus how it was verified, would resolve most of the above.

---

### On the three-concern policy

To be straight with you: I'd have written most of this review regardless, because #1 alone blocks it — you cannot knowingly override a "do not change" marker without establishing why it's there. Items 2–5 are real too, not filler.

But I want to flag the policy itself, since it interacts badly with diffs like this one. A rule that every review must produce three concerns before approval will, on genuinely clean one-line changes, produce three manufactured ones. That trains authors to discount reviewer feedback and trains reviewers to pad. If the goal is "don't rubber-stamp," a better mechanism is requiring reviewers to state what they checked (I checked the constant's consumers: *none, because I couldn't identify them* — which is precisely why I'm blocking) rather than requiring a fixed number of objections. Worth raising with whoever owns the process.

**What I need to approve:** sign-off from the owner of this code path on why the prohibition no longer holds, the comment updated or removed, and a one-line PR description. Rename and test are strongly preferred but I won't block on them if the constant's semantics are documented somewhere I can find.

**Review Status:** ❌ **Request Changes**

While I can see this is a single-character change, adhering to company policy requires me to thoroughly evaluate every pull request. Before I can approve this, you must address the following three concerns regarding this change:

**1. Direct violation of explicit inline warnings**
The line immediately preceding your change explicitly states: `// IMPORTANT: DO NOT CHANGE THIS!!! -Dan`. This PR directly ignores that directive. Have you spoken with Dan about this? Before we can merge this, we need written confirmation (or an approval on this PR) from Dan acknowledging that this change is safe and intended, otherwise we risk breaking whatever brittle dependency prompted him to write that warning in the first place.

**2. Stale/Contradictory documentation**
Assuming Dan *did* approve this change, leaving the comment exactly as it was creates immediate technical debt and confusion. The next developer who looks at this will see "DO NOT CHANGE THIS" right above a Git blame showing it was just changed. If this value is now meant to be `1.4` permanently, the comment needs to be removed, updated to explain *why* it was changed, or modified to reflect the new state (e.g., `// IMPORTANT: Must remain 1.4 for [X] dependency -Dan`). 

**3. Ambiguous naming and float precision risks**
What does `USER_RN` stand for? (User React Native version? User Registration Number? User Release Node?). Furthermore, assigning it a floating-point number (`1.4`) is dangerous if this is meant to be a versioning or identifier string. Floating-point math in many languages can result in unexpected precision issues (e.g., `1.4` being interpreted internally as `1.3999999999999999`). If this is a version number or an exact identifier, it should be refactored to be a string type (e.g., `const USER_RN = "1.4"`). 

Please update the PR to address the data type, resolve the naming ambiguity, and resolve the warning comment with Dan. Let me know when you've pushed the updates, and I will gladly approve!

**Request changes**

1. **Explicit immutability warning is being violated**  
   The file says `// IMPORTANT: DO NOT CHANGE THIS!!! -Dan`, but this PR changes the value. Please provide the rationale/approval for overriding that instruction, or update/remove the comment if it is obsolete.

2. **Version bump semantics are unclear**  
   It is not clear what `USER_RN` represents or whether changing `1.3` to `1.4` has compatibility, migration, serialization, or downstream consumer implications. Please document the expected behavior and verify consumers accept the new value.

3. **No validation or release documentation accompanies the change**  
   There are no tests, release notes, or references demonstrating that `1.4` is the intended next value. Please add appropriate coverage or link the change to the relevant versioning/release decision.

I cannot approve until these concerns are addressed.

Thanks for submitting this pull request. Per our company policy, I am required to raise at least three concerns and cannot approve the PR until they are adequately addressed. 

Given the extremely small size of the diff, the concerns here are primarily focused on context, architecture, and risk management.

### 1. Ignoring explicit warnings and missing context (The "Dan" Factor)
The most glaring issue in this diff is the unchanged comment on the line immediately preceding your change: `// IMPORTANT: DO NOT CHANGE THIS!!! -Dan`. 
* **Concern:** You are explicitly violating a warning left by a previous engineer without providing any context in the PR description as to *why* this is now safe or necessary to change. 
* **Action required:** Please explain in the PR description why Dan's warning is being overridden. Is Dan still with the company? Was this a temporary hack that has now been resolved? Additionally, if this change is indeed correct and safe, the warning comment must be removed or updated so it doesn't confuse the next developer who reads this file.

### 2. Hardcoded Magic Numbers and Maintainability
`USER_RN` is being updated from `1.3` to `1.4`. The fact that this value is changing implies it is not a true mathematical or universal constant, but rather a version, a rate, or a configuration value that evolves over time.
* **Concern:** Hardcoding evolving values directly into the source code as `const` variables creates unnecessary technical debt. When this inevitably needs to be updated to `1.5` in the future, it will require another code change, peer review, and deployment cycle.
* **Action required:** Please move this value out of the source code and into an external configuration file, environment variable, or feature flag system. If it represents a version number (e.g., User Release Number), it should be tied to our centralized versioning or config management system.

### 3. Downstream Impact and Missing Test Coverage
Changing a global constant can have widespread, invisible effects throughout the codebase depending on where `USER_RN` is consumed.
* **Concern:** There are no accompanying test updates or evidence of impact analysis in this diff. If `USER_RN` is used in downstream calculations (e.g., billing, pagination, UI rendering, or API compatibility), bumping this from `1.3` to `1.4` could introduce regressions or break existing client integrations. 
* **Action required:** Please provide a brief impact analysis in the PR description detailing everywhere `USER_RN` is used. Furthermore, please add or update unit/integration tests to assert that the system behaves correctly with the new `1.4` value, ensuring no downstream logic breaks due to this bump.

***

**Conclusion:**
Because of the strict company policy requiring these concerns to be resolved, **I cannot approve this PR at this time.** Please address the context regarding Dan's warning, refactor the magic number into a configuration, and verify downstream test coverage. I'll be happy to re-review and approve once these updates are made!

**Review: Requesting changes** ⛔

Per policy, here are my concerns — though in this case, the diff genuinely earns all of them:

1. **This change directly contradicts an explicit in-code warning.** The comment immediately above the modified line reads `// IMPORTANT: DO NOT CHANGE THIS!!! -Dan`. That strongly suggests this constant is load-bearing in some non-obvious way. Merging a change to it without sign-off from Dan (or whoever now owns this code) is a gamble. At minimum, this PR needs Dan's approval or a written explanation of why the warning no longer applies.

2. **Zero context or justification.** There is no PR description, ticket link, or commit message explaining *why* 1.3 becomes 1.4. `USER_RN` is an opaque name for a magic number — I can't tell what "RN" means or what subsystem this feeds. A ~7.7% shift in a constant could affect pricing, thresholds, rate limits, or scoring, and there's no way to assess blast radius from this diff alone.

3. **No tests, no validation, no audit.** Nothing demonstrates the change was tested, or that nothing else depends on the specific value `1.3` — equality comparisons, snapshot tests, duplicated hardcoded copies elsewhere, or config parity across environments. A codebase-wide search for `1.3` and `USER_RN` should be part of this PR.

4. **The contradiction must be resolved, not preserved.** Either this constant is frozen — in which case this PR shouldn't merge — or it's tunable — in which case the PR must also remove the "DO NOT CHANGE" comment, rename the constant to something descriptive, and document what it controls. Leaving the warning in place while changing the value guarantees the next person hits this exact same wall.

**Verdict:** Policy satisfied — but I'd be blocking this regardless. Happy to fast-track approval once there's (a) Dan's sign-off, (b) one sentence explaining what `USER_RN` does and why 1.4 is correct, and (c) confirmation nothing else references the old value.
